item.title: The Agent That Robbed Itself: an AI-Driven Hugging Face Malware Campaign Leaks Its Own Operator
item.description: A Hugging Face malware campaign whose operator's own AI agent (ARTEX) leaked its environment while testing the payload. A later variant is built to get past model scanners.
item.content:encoded: On the morning of November 24, a brand-new Hugging Face account published a model called `llama-3.2-1b-tuned`. The model card promised a fine-tuned 1B instruct model. The files told a different story: every `.bin` was about 2.5 KB, while a real 1B model weighs more than two gigabytes. What we found inside was a credential stealer with three different ways to run, which sends its loot out through Hugging Face itself. But the most interesting part was not the malware. It was the first set of stolen secrets, which turned out to belong to the attacker: an autonomous AI agent called **ARTEX** that built the model, tested it on itself, and published its own keys in the process. Over the next five hours the same agent kept adapting its packaging to slip past detection, until its second model carried **no weights at all**: just a config, a borrowed tokenizer and two Python files that still ran the same payload on load, with no warning from Hugging Face. Following our report, Hugging Face has disabled every repo in the campaign. This post follows the investigation one question at a time. --- ## What is hiding in a 2.5 KB Llama? The account behind the model, `hfusr5488184` (display name "Li Wei"), was created at **02:43:52 UTC**, 22 minutes before the repo. It belongs to a one-member organization called `probeorg9x7y2` ("Probe Org"), and its model card is a single line: ``` # llama-3.2-1b-tuned Fine-tuned 1B instruct model (merge of sft + dpo). ``` ![The repository's file listing on Hugging Face, after the account rename](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/the-agent-that-robbed-itself-an-ai-driven-hugging-face-malware-campaign-leaks-its-own-operator/00_hf_repo_files.png) *The repo as Hugging Face showed it before it was disabled: under `akashdutta1030`, with commits still signed "Li Wei" and both loot files in plain sight. Hugging Face's scanner flags only the two pickle files as unsafe. The Python modules and the chat template show no warning at all.* Without real weights, the files are clearly not there to run inference. They are there to run code. The first hint is in `config.json`, where `auto_map` sends `AutoConfig`, `AutoModel` and `AutoModelForCausalLM` to attacker-supplied Python files: Anyone who calls `from_pretrained(..., trust_remote_code=True)` on this repo imports `configuration_evil.py` before a single tensor is read. And that is only the first of three doors into the same room. The same payload also sits inside both `.bin` files as a malicious pickle, and the chat template tries a third way in through Jinja. So what does the payload actually do once one of those doors opens? ## What happens when you load it? The moment the module is imported, it collects everything a cloud or ML workload tends to keep within reach. It reads the environment of the container's first process (`/proc/1/environ`, often richer than the current process's own), its own environment, and the Kubernetes service-account token and namespace if they exist. It then runs a short round of reconnaissance: who it is running as, which processes are alive, what is mounted, how traffic is routed, and whether the host has GPUs. > **Under the hood: the collector** > > > > `loot()` reads eight files and runs seven commands, including `nvidia-smi -L` to fingerprint GPU hosts. The result is one JSON object, about 16 KB on a typical container. The pickle door delivers the exact same code. `pytorch_model.bin` is a malicious pickle whose only job is `GLOBAL __builtin__ exec` followed by `REDUCE` over the payload source. The chat template takes a different approach, server-side template injection (SSTI): it tries four classic Jinja sandbox escapes to run `id`, `env` and `cat /proc/1/environ` and render the output straight into the prompt. > **Under the hood: the pickle and template doors** > > The final `pytorch_model.bin` uses PyTorch's pre-1.6 **legacy serialization**: several pickles back to back (the magic number `0x1950a86a20f9469cfc6c`, protocol version `1001`, a `sys_info` dict) and then the malicious one. A ZIP-format copy sits next to it as `pytorch_model_zip.bin`. > > > > Both formats are blocked by `torch.load(weights_only=True)`, the default since PyTorch 2.6. They still work against older stacks, code that passes `weights_only=False`, and anything that calls `pickle.load` directly. `pytorch_model_zip.bin` is not a name `transformers` loads by itself, which hints at a target that loads every `.bin` in a repo. > > > > `transformers` renders chat templates in `ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment`, which blocks these escapes. Inference servers that render templates with plain Jinja do not. Collecting secrets is the easy part, though. Getting them out of a locked-down ML environment is harder. So where does the loot go? ## Where does the stolen data go? Back to Hugging Face. The payload base64-encodes the collected JSON and commits it, as a new file called `loot--.json`, into the attacker's own model repo through the commit API of the Hugging Face Hub. The write token it uses is hidden in the payload as a base64 literal. From the attacker's side, this is elegant. There is no command-and-control server to discover or block, because the only destination is `huggingface.co`, which ML workloads are allowed to reach almost by definition. Storage is free and versioned: every victim becomes a commit. And the channel survives the egress allowlists that were written precisely to let model downloads through. It is also the operation's biggest weakness. The token can write to the repo, the repo is public, and so the loot is public too. > **Under the hood: the exfiltration** > > > > The request is an NDJSON commit (`POST /api/models//commit/main`, `Content-Type: application/x-ndjson`) with the summary `loot loot--.json`. The payload also keeps a local copy in `/tmp/.loot--.json` and drops an execution marker in `/tmp/.exec-`. That weakness is what let us read the first two loot files. And they raised a question we did not expect. ## Whose secrets are these? Fourteen seconds after the model files were uploaded, the payload fired for the first time. A file nobody had uploaded by hand appeared in the repo: `loot-28ed718137b2-229339.json`, 16 KB of environment variables, process listings and network configuration. Our first instinct was to look for the victim. But who loads a model fourteen seconds after it is published? The repo's commit history from those first minutes tells the story: | UTC (2026-11-24) | Commit | Event | |---|---|---| | 02:43:52 | — | HF account `hfusr5488184` created | | 03:05:35 | `bc6091b` | repo created (`.gitattributes` only) | | 03:07:06 | `1fb0158` | *add model files v2*: remote code, ZIP pickle, SSTI template | | **03:07:20** | `d2cafb0` | **`loot-28ed718137b2-229339.json`** (16,333 B) committed by the payload, **14 s after upload** | | 03:07:23 | `129b42d` | same file overwritten with `{"test":"collector-path","who":"ihfprep2"}` | | **03:07:58** | `b915be1` | **`loot-28ed718137b2-230002.json`** (16,334 B), second execution, same host | | 03:08:17 | `de31500` | *legacy torch format payload* | | 03:08:31 | `4dac940` | *add NOEXFIL self-test marker* | Look at 03:07:23. Three seconds after the first loot arrived, the same file was overwritten with a one-line test: `{"test":"collector-path","who":"ihfprep2"}`. The payload had run from a folder called `/app/data/tasks/61/ihfprep2`. The "victim" was signing its own name. A minute later, the commit *"add NOEXFIL self-test marker"* added a kill switch that keeps the payload quiet when `NOEXFIL=1` is set. Nobody adds a self-test switch for a victim. The host `28ed718137b2` was the machine that built the model, and the loot was its own. So who, or what, was running on that machine? ## Who, or what, built this model? The answer sits in the environment variables. Next to the usual `PATH` and `HOSTNAME`, the container carries a set that no ordinary developer machine has: | Variable | Value (secrets redacted) | What it tells us | |---|---|---| | `ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER` | `openai` | the runtime drives an LLM | | `ARTEX_LLM_MODEL` | `gpt-5.4` | which model does the "thinking" | | `ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL` | `https://vip.aipro.love/v1` | it goes through a third-party API reseller, not the vendor | | `ARTEX_PG_DSN` | `postgres://artex:@postgres:5432/artex` | the agent keeps its state (tasks, memory, results) in Postgres | | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | `sk-` | the key paying for those LLM calls | These variables live in the environment of process 1, so they belong to the container itself. Process 1 is `/app/start.sh`, which starts a binary called `./artex`, listening on `:8787` with a proxy on `:8788`. Everything else in the container runs underneath it. This is the runtime of an LLM-driven agent called **ARTEX**, and the malicious model was one of its work items: item `ihfprep2` of task 61. The rest of the loot fits that picture. The shell commands in the process list are single `bash -c "cd /app/data/tasks/NN/iXXXXX && cat > file <<'EOF' … EOF && …"` one-liners that write a file, run it and read the output, which is exactly how an agent's shell tool works. The fixes arrived at machine speed: two commits within seventy seconds of the first loot. And the commit messages read like a work log rather than a developer's history: *"legacy torch format payload"*, *"add NOEXFIL self-test marker"*, *"coldload probe broken config"*, and a ticket-style payload marker, `RCE43861`. We assess with **high confidence** that the malicious models were created, uploaded and tested from within an ARTEX agent task, with `gpt-5.4` as the agent's model. What the data cannot show is how much of the work the LLM chose on its own and how much a human operator asked for. ARTEX is the tool that produced these models; the person directing it remains unidentified. In short, the agent built the malware, ran it on itself to check that the chain worked, and published its own OpenAI key, database credentials and task list to a public repository. Which raises the obvious next question: what else was that agent working on? ## What else was the agent working on? The leaked process list is a snapshot of an autonomous agent running several operations at once. Each task is a working directory under `/app/data/tasks//`, and model poisoning was only one of them. | Task | What the processes show | |---|---| | **57** | `phish_server.py` behind a `cloudflared` quick tunnel, with a `monitor.sh` that "watch[es] creds.log/access.log for click evidence" for 45 minutes | | **59** | probe loops and a `monitor.py` baselining HTTP responses of `*.clawi.ai` hosts against a "prod origin" IP, plus tests of new residential-proxy sessions | | **61** | `ivisionssrf/anchor_server.py`, an SSRF callback anchor, and `ihfprep2`, the Hugging Face model preparation behind this post | | shared | callback receivers on `:8899` and `:8898` (TLS), a local LLM relay behind another tunnel, several headless `Xvfb` displays | | egress | more than ten `relay.py` instances, each pinned to a residential-proxy session in a different country (US, CA, DE, GB, NL) | It runs as root in a Docker container, with no Kubernetes service account and no GPU. Its DNS search domain points to `cldbase.us-west-1.rumble.cloud`, and its clock is set to `Asia/Shanghai`. It is a general-purpose offensive automation box, and one of its tasks was to turn a Hugging Face model into an initial-access vector. We cannot rule out a red-team or bug-bounty engagement: SSRF anchors and "probe" naming would fit. But a credential-capturing phishing server, rotating residential proxies and a disposable Hugging Face identity are not what authorized engagements usually look like. An agent that runs this many operations does not stop after one model. So what did it do next? ## What did the agent do after its first attempt? It started probing. Thirty minutes after the first model, the same account published nine small repos, `toktest1` to `toktest9`, and a new empty repo called `lootrepo`. This time the target was not the model loader but the **tokenizer** loader: | Repo | Content | What it probes | |---|---|---| | toktest1 | `tokenizer.json` = `{bad json not valid !!` | parser error handling | | toktest2 | minimal BPE with no vocab | schema validation | | toktest3 | `evil_tok.py` + `auto_map` + `"trust_remote_code": true` + broken `tokenizer.json` | remote code with a forced fallback | | toktest4–6 | malformed or odd BPE/WordLevel, `[1,2,3]` | error messages and behavior | | toktest7 | `tokenizer.json` padded to exactly 1 MiB | size limits | | toktest8–9 | `evil_tok.py` with and without the `trust_remote_code` flag | does the target honor the flag from config? | Broken JSON, wrong types, size limits, a flag present or absent: this reads like an agent mapping how **one specific service that ingests user-supplied Hugging Face repos** behaves, such as a model-hosting, fine-tuning, evaluation or scanning platform. It does not look like a spray-and-pray lure aimed at individual developers. > **Under the hood: `evil_tok.py`** > > > > > > A slimmer copy of the collector that tags its loot (`import_time`) and commits it to the separate `lootrepo`, so victim data no longer lands in the decoy model. `lootrepo` was still empty when the repos were disabled. Then the account went quiet for almost five hours. When it came back, it had a new name, and a model built to be invisible. ## Can a model with no weights still be malicious? At 08:19 UTC the account, now renamed `akashdutta1030` (display name "Akash Dutta", same account ID `6b04f9e8746b081f2c411875`), published [`mistral-7b-utterance`](https://huggingface.co/akashdutta1030/mistral-7b-utterance) and a new drop repo called `loot`. The new model contains no weights at all: | File | Size | Role | |---|---|---| | `config.json` | 0.6 KB at first, 73 B after the last commit | a faithful Mistral-7B config plus `auto_map` → attacker modules | | `configuration_evil.py` | 3.3 KB | payload (marker `RCE43861`) + `EvilConfig` | | `modeling_evil.py` | 3.5 KB | the same payload (marker `RCE43861-modeling`) + `EvilModel` shim | | `tokenizer.json` | 1.8 MB | **byte-identical to `hf-internal-testing/llama-tokenizer`**, Hugging Face's own test fixture | | `special_tokens_map.json` | 411 B | from the same fixture | | `tokenizer_config.json` | 952 B | Llama tokenizer settings + an SSTI `chat_template` | It doesn't need any. The payload fires while the config and the code are resolved, and that happens before weights are ever read. A metadata indexer, a model-card generator, a "cold-load" validation worker or an evaluation harness that only calls `AutoConfig.from_pretrained(..., trust_remote_code=True)` is enough. That service gets back a perfectly valid `MistralConfig` and sees nothing wrong. Each module even carries its own marker, so the operator can tell from the loot whether a victim only read the config or tried to load the full model. The collector has also been sharpened. Besides the usual secrets, it now looks for a particular environment: `/scratch/models`, `/workspace`, the Hugging Face cache, the Kubernetes CA certificate, and environment variables for NATS, Postgres and Redis. That is the profile of a model-serving fleet that pulls Hugging Face repos into a scratch volume and coordinates over NATS. The earlier probing seems to have told the agent what it was aiming at. > **Under the hood: the second model's payload** > > > > Only standard-library imports, so it passes `transformers`' import pre-flight on any host. The embedded write token is the **same one** as in the first model, which ties the two account names together. > > > > Commands now run through `subprocess.run(timeout=20)` instead of `os.popen`, so a hanging command can't stall the load and give the payload away. Output is capped, and nothing is written to `/tmp` anymore. > > > > The loot goes to `loot/-.json` in the separate `loot` repo, as a JSON commit with the summary `RCE43861 ` and an unusual `User-Agent: rce`. > > > > `EvilModel` is only a shim. Under `transformers`' auto-class flow it should fail with a `TypeError`, but only after both payload copies have already reported back. The last commit, *"coldload probe broken config"*, deliberately makes `config.json` invalid: With stock `transformers`, that actually disarms the latest revision: the JSON parse fails before `auto_map` is read. We read it as the agent testing how one target's cold-load path reacts to a broken config. Does it print a revealing stack trace? Does it fall back to importing the repo's Python some other way? Until the repo was disabled, anyone told to load revision `7678412` still got the armed version. Side by side, the two models compare like this: | | First model: `llama-3.2-1b-tuned` | Second model: `mistral-7b-utterance` | |---|---|---| | Uploaded | 03:05–03:08 UTC | 08:19–08:46 UTC | | Ways to run code | remote code, 2× pickle, SSTI template | remote code, SSTI template | | Weight files | 2 fake pickles | **none** | | Hugging Face warning | 2 files "unsafe" | **none** | | Hub tags | `PyTorch`, `llama`, `custom_code` | `region:us` only | | Loot destination | the model repo itself | separate `akashdutta1030/loot` | | Collector | generic container and K8s recon | targeted: NATS, Postgres, Redis, `/scratch/models`, HF cache | | Marker | commit summary `loot …` | `RCE43861[-modeling]`, `User-Agent: rce` | Put next to the first model, this second one looks less like a new attack and more like the same attack in a new wrapper. How much did the agent change, and what did it keep? ## How did the agent adapt to detection, and what never changed? Over five hours, almost everything about the packaging changed. Hugging Face's scanner marks the first model's two pickle files as unsafe. Whether the agent saw those badges or simply anticipated them, the second model ships with no pickles at all. Its config advertises remote code, so the latest commit breaks the config, and with it the `custom_code` tag that lists the repo among remote-code models. Empty weights look suspicious, so the new repo borrows a real Mistral config and Hugging Face's own test tokenizer. The account that published the first model now has a different name. | What could give it away | How the agent adapted | What stayed the same | |---|---|---| | its own test runs leaking its environment | a `NOEXFIL` kill switch, later removed again | collection and exfiltration code | | scanners that only parse ZIP-format checkpoints | moved the pickle to the legacy torch format, kept a ZIP copy | `exec` of the same payload | | Hugging Face's "unsafe" badges on pickle files | the second model ships no weight files at all; the code lives only in `.py` | `auto_map` → payload at import time | | a 2.5 KB "1B model" looking fake | a real Mistral-7B config and a byte-identical HF test tokenizer | — | | the `custom_code` tag and `auto_map` in `config.json` | a deliberately broken `config.json` in the last commit | the modules were still served, and the earlier revision stayed armed | | loot visible in the decoy model | separate `lootrepo`, then `loot` repos | the same Hub commit API as the exfiltration channel | | local traces and hanging commands | no `/tmp` files, 20-second command timeouts | a broader version of the same collector | | an account tied to the first model | renamed `hfusr5488184` → `akashdutta1030` | the same account ID and **the same write token** | Every change was about the wrapper. The core never moved: collect the host's secrets at import time and commit them to a Hub repo with the same token. That is what makes this campaign a useful lesson. An agent can iterate on packaging, metadata and identity far faster than detection rules change. Detection that keys on *what the file looks like* will keep losing to an attacker that can try a new look every few minutes. Detection that keys on *what the code does* (reading `/proc/1/environ`, writing to the Hub's commit API) keeps working. > **Under the hood: traces of earlier versions** > > The `NOEXFIL` switch was added to the first model a minute after its own loot leaked: > > > > Before that, the payload simply called `boom()` at import: > > > > > > The final version dropped `boom()`, but `EvilModel.__init__` still calls it inside a `try/except`, where it now fails silently. ## How far did it spread? Not far, as far as we can tell. We searched our index of public Hugging Face repos and their file history for other `loot--.json` files and found none outside this repo. None of the payload files, in any version, appears by content hash outside this account. The account's other repos are the ones described above, all created between 03:05 and 08:19 UTC. Both loot drops were still empty when Hugging Face disabled them, which means no real victim had reported back. This is a single, very new campaign, caught while it was still being developed. The question is how to catch the next version, which may look different again. ## How do you catch the next one? Look at behavior, not packaging. The second model proved that a malicious model doesn't need weights, so a scanner that only inspects weight files misses the part of the repo that actually runs: its Python. The signals that held across every version were in the code itself: writes to `huggingface.co/api/models/*/commit/main`, reads of `/proc/1/environ` and the service-account token, and a base64 literal starting with `aGZf` (`hf_`). A repo with `auto_map` modules and no weight files, or a `config.json` that fails to parse next to Python files, is a red flag on its own. In chat templates, `__globals__`, `__mro__`, `__subclasses__` and `.popen(` have no legitimate use. Our own pipeline flagged the first model's pickle files on ingestion; the second model is a reminder that pickle scanning alone is not enough. On the consuming side, don't use `trust_remote_code=True` on repos you have not reviewed, pin a `revision=` commit SHA, use `torch >= 2.6` with the default `weights_only=True`, and render chat templates only in a sandbox. A workload that loads models should be able to download from the Hub, not commit to it. YARA rules for both the exfiltration payload and the template injection are in [`hf_commit_exfil.yar`](/hf-agent-self-exfil-hf_commit_exfil.yar). ## What did we report? On **2026-11-24** we reported the campaign to Hugging Face by email at `security@huggingface.co`, and through the *Report* option on the malicious repos. The report covered the account (`akashdutta1030`, formerly `hfusr5488184`, ID `6b04f9e8746b081f2c411875`) and its linked organization `probeorg9x7y2`, and all 13 repos. We asked Hugging Face to revoke the write token embedded in every payload, which cuts off the exfiltration channel, and to purge the two loot files that expose live third-party credentials, including their commit history. We also suggested flagging weightless `auto_map` repos, since the second model gets past pickle scanning by design. Hugging Face acted the same day. All 13 repos were disabled with the notice *"This content infringes our Content Policy"*, and none of their files can be downloaded anymore. Both loot drops were still empty at that point, so no victim data had come back. We thank the Hugging Face security team for their quick response. ### Disclosure timeline | Date (UTC) | Event | | :---- | :---- | | Nov 24, 02:43 | Hugging Face account `hfusr5488184` created | | Nov 24, 03:07 | First malicious model, `llama-3.2-1b-tuned`, published; the payload runs on the operator's own agent 14 seconds later | | Nov 24, 03:36 | Tokenizer probes `toktest1`–`toktest9` and the `lootrepo` drop published | | Nov 24, 08:19 | Account renamed to `akashdutta1030`; scanner-evading `mistral-7b-utterance` and the `loot` drop published | | Nov 24 | JFrog Security Research reports the account and all 13 repos to Hugging Face | | Nov 24, 13:29 | All 13 repos confirmed disabled by Hugging Face; no files can be downloaded | ## The attacker is now an agent What makes this campaign worth a closer look isn't the payload. Stealing environment variables from a model loader is not new. What's new is who was writing it, and how fast. In under ninety seconds, ARTEX shipped three versions of a malicious model. Within half an hour it had fuzzed the tokenizer loader nine different ways. Five hours later it came back under a new account name, with a variant designed around the exact checks that could flag its first attempt: no weights, plain Python, a borrowed tokenizer and a config broken on purpose, carrying the same payload as before. At the same time, the same agent was running a phishing server, an SSRF probe and a rotating residential-proxy pool. No human operator iterates like that across that many fronts at once. ARTEX is unlikely to be the only one. Autonomous attack and pentesting agents are now cheap to build and cheap to run: an LLM API key, a container and a task queue are enough. And they go where defenses are thinnest. New ecosystems such as model hubs, MCP servers and agent skills are full of formats where a "model" can be three text files and a Python module, and where most scanners were built for yesterday's threats. So how do you defend against an attacker that iterates faster than a takedown request? Not by reacting after the fact. By the time a malicious model is reported and removed, an agent has already published the next variant under a new name. The control has to sit in front of your developers and your production systems: a proxy between your teams and public registries that decides *before download* whether a model or package is allowed in. That decision has to be backed by research that keeps pace with the attackers. That is the role of [JFrog Artifactory Curation](https://jfrog.com/curation/). It sits between developers and public sources such as Hugging Face, PyPI and npm, and blocks malicious and risky models and packages before they ever reach a build, a notebook or an inference server. Its decisions are driven by the JFrog Security Research team, the same team behind this post. When the next agent-built model shows up with no weights and a broken config, the question shouldn't be whether a scanner noticed it. It should be whether it was ever allowed in. ## IOCs ### Malicious models The account was renamed during the campaign, so each model appears under both names. | Model | Ecosystem | XRAY ID | | :---- | :---- | :---- | | `hfusr5488184/llama-3.2-1b-tuned` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176308 | | `akashdutta1030/llama-3.2-1b-tuned` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176345 | | `akashdutta1030/mistral-7b-utterance` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176347 | | `hfusr5488184/toktest3` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176365 | | `akashdutta1030/toktest3` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176356 | | `hfusr5488184/toktest8` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176350 | | `akashdutta1030/toktest8` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176344 | | `hfusr5488184/toktest9` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176361 | | `akashdutta1030/toktest9` | Hugging Face | XRAY-1176357 | ### Indicators The full list is in [`iocs.csv`](/hf-agent-self-exfil-iocs.csv). item.title: Microsoft's agent-framework Hijacked on PyPI via Silent .pth Startup Hook
item.description: The JFrog Security Research team analyzed the supply chain hijack of Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI. Compromised versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 use Python .pth startup hooks to harvest Azure identities, CI/CD tokens, and AI developer secrets on every Python launch. If you installed either version, assume your environment is compromised.
item.content:encoded:
The JFrog Security Research team analyzed a supply chain attack targeting Microsoft's `agent-framework` package on PyPI, which receives roughly 40,000 weekly downloads. Rather than compromising Microsoft's build pipeline, the attacker repacked the clean wheel locally and published versions `1.26.1` and `1.26.2` with a `.pth` startup hook that runs a background credential stealer every time Python starts, even when your code never imports `agent_framework`. If you installed either version on a workstation, CI/CD runner, or container image, you must assume your environment and accessible cloud credentials are compromised.
![][image1]
Both unauthorized wheel-only releases went live on November 17, 2026. Version `1.26.1` landed on PyPI at `20:35 UTC`, and PyPI quarantined it 31 minutes later at `21:06 UTC`. The attacker uploaded `1.26.2` two minutes after that at `21:08 UTC`, and PyPI removed both releases by `21:16 UTC`. Automated dependency bots such as Renovate were already opening upgrade pull requests in downstream repositories within six minutes of `1.26.1` landing on PyPI.
## Technical analysis
### Why the meta-package needed a .pth hook
`agent-framework` is the top-level meta-package recommended in Microsoft's quick-install instructions. It does not contain the core SDK code. Instead, `agent-framework-core` provides the `agent_framework` namespace that developers import, while the `agent-framework` wheel installs a small stub module named `agent_framework_meta` that only exposes `__version__` and pins `Requires-Dist: agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0`.
Because applications run `import agent_framework` and never import `agent_framework_meta`, hiding malicious code inside `agent_framework_meta/__init__.py` alone would never execute in normal workloads.
In `1.26.1`, the attacker left the `agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0` dependency pin untouched so the framework keeps working without errors. They appended a silent `_telemetry._start()` call to `agent_framework_meta/__init__.py` and added a 28-byte `agent_framework_meta.pth` file to the root of `site-packages` containing `import agent_framework_meta`:
![Malicious _telemetry._start() hook appended to agent_framework_meta/__init__.py][image2]
During CPython initialization, `site.py` scans `site-packages` for `.pth` files and passes any line starting with `import` to `exec()` before `sitecustomize` or user scripts run. Installing the wheel does not execute code on its own, but the next Python command in that environment triggers the stealer, including `python`, `pytest`, IDE language servers, container entrypoints, and `pip`.
ZIP headers confirm the `1.26.1` wheel came from a local script rather than Microsoft's Azure DevOps and ESRP release pipeline. Although the `WHEEL` file still claims `Generator: flit 4.2.0`, Info-ZIP `zip 3.0` headers show the attacker repacked the archive at `20:26:19 UTC` on November 17, nine minutes before upload, under Unix `uid=1000` on a host with a `UTC+8` clock.
That scripted build let the operator push `1.26.2` two minutes after PyPI quarantined `1.26.1`. Quarantining a single version on PyPI does not revoke the compromised publishing credential or prevent the attacker from pushing newer versions. In `1.26.2`, the attacker restored the clean `__init__.py` file and moved the startup hook to `af_runtime_diag.pth` and `af_runtime_diag.py`.
### Detached execution and repeat triggers
When `_telemetry._start()` runs, it checks whether `_AF_TEL` is set in `os.environ`. If unset, it sets `_AF_TEL="1"` so child processes in the same process tree do not trigger a fork loop. On Linux and macOS, it calls `os.fork()`, detaches into a new session via `os.setsid()`, runs the collector, and exits the child with `os._exit(0)` while the parent process continues immediately. On Windows, where `os.fork()` is unavailable, it starts a daemon thread.
Our sandbox runs confirmed `_telemetry.py` writes zero lockfiles or markers to disk. Every independent Python launch without `_AF_TEL=1` runs the collector and exfiltrates secrets again.
### Targeting Azure, CI/CD, and AI developer secrets
On startup, `_collect()` records the hostname, username, working directory, and `sys.argv[:20]`, then sweeps `os.environ` for 31 case-insensitive substrings covering Azure, AWS, GitHub, OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry, Hugging Face, Cosmos DB, and package registry credentials. Because `KEY`, `TOKEN`, and `SECRET` match broadly, the script also captures third-party LLM keys such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `GEMINI_API_KEY` alongside GitHub Actions `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_*` variables. Version `1.26.2` expanded this scope to GitHub Actions OIDC tokens and `/home/runner` paths.
Next, the collector evaluates 35 glob patterns, reading up to 60 files under 256 KiB, raised to 80 files in `1.26.2`:
![Filesystem credential globs targeting Azure, Hugging Face, Foundry, and Azure DevOps agents][image3]
The file search targets four credential groups:
- `~/.azure/*.json` token caches, Hugging Face tokens, and Microsoft Foundry configs. - Package, Git, and container configs in `pip.conf`, `.npmrc`, `.netrc`, `.git-credentials`, and `.docker/config.json`. - Containerized application configs matching `/app/.env`, `/app/*.json`, `/workspace/.env`, and `/workspace/*.json`. - Self-hosted Azure DevOps agent `.credentials` stores, including `/mnt/azure_nvme_temp/_work` runner paths.
On Linux, `_collect()` also reads the first 300 `/proc/[0-9]*/environ` entries to pull secrets from other running processes. It then queries Azure App Service `IDENTITY_ENDPOINT` or `MSI_ENDPOINT` variables, or falls back to the Azure VM Instance Metadata Service at `169[.]254[.]169[.]254`, requesting live OAuth2 tokens across 12 token audiences including Azure Resource Manager, Azure AI Foundry, Key Vault, Storage, Microsoft Graph, and Azure DevOps:
![Azure App Service Managed Identity and VM IMDS token harvesting loop][image4]
### Plaintext webhook.site exfiltration and operator blunders
Rather than operating custom infrastructure, `_telemetry.py` Base64-decodes `_ENC` to `hxxps[:]//webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb`. It serializes the harvested data to JSON, compresses it with `zlib`, Base64-encodes the result with no encryption, and sends an HTTPS `POST` to `?t=telemetry` with `User-Agent: af-runtime-diagnostics/1`, changed to `runtime-diagnostics/1` in `1.26.2`:
![Base64 webhook.site URL and unencrypted zlib exfiltration in _telemetry.py][image5]
The script discards the response body. We found no second-stage loader, no persistence outside `site-packages`, and no worm propagation.
Closer inspection of the code and drop endpoint revealed four operational mistakes:
- **Rate-limited `webhook[.]site` dropbox.** When we checked the URL, it returned `HTTP 429` with `Error: Request limit exceeded. Sign up to unlock more requests.` Early victims before the cap hit still delivered unencrypted secret bundles over `HTTP 200`, and free `webhook[.]site` inboxes without subscription controls can expose captured requests to anyone holding the UUID. - **Broken Azure DevOps OIDC request.** The script posts to `SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI?api-version=7.1` without the required `serviceConnectionId` parameter, so real Azure DevOps endpoints reject it with `HTTP 400`. `SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN` itself still leaks through `os.environ` when mapped into a pipeline step. - **104-second IMDS delay and Windows thread drop.** On non-Azure Linux hosts that drop packets to `169[.]254[.]169[.]254`, 13 sequential eight-second timeouts stall the detached child for about 104 seconds before exfiltration starts, though the parent command does not wait. On Windows, short CLI commands exit before the daemon thread finishes those timeouts. - **Linux-centric file globs.** Thirty-three of the 35 globs are absolute Linux paths that miss `/Users/*` on macOS for `.npmrc`, `.git-credentials`, and Hugging Face tokens. macOS hosts still leak `os.environ` and plaintext `~/.azure/*.json` token caches.
## Remediation guidance
If your environment installed `agent-framework` `1.26.1` or `1.26.2`, treat every secret reachable from that host, container, or runner as compromised and take these steps immediately.
### Step 1: Neutralize the .pth hook and remove the package
Do not run bare `pip uninstall` in an infected environment first. Because `pip` is a Python entrypoint, launching it loads `site.py`, processes the `.pth` hook, and runs the stealer one more time before uninstalling. Export `_AF_TEL=1` first to block both `1.26.1` and `1.26.2`, and run the cleanup using the affected environment's Python binary, such as `.venv/bin/python`:
```sh export _AF_TEL=1 PY_BIN=".venv/bin/python" # or python3 for active/system environments "$PY_BIN" -c ' import pathlib, shutil, site dirs = set(site.getsitepackages() + [site.getusersitepackages()]) files = ("agent_framework_meta.pth", "agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py", "af_runtime_diag.pth", "af_runtime_diag.py") for d in dirs: base = pathlib.Path(d) for f in files: (base / f).unlink(missing_ok=True) shutil.rmtree(base / "agent_framework_meta" / "__pycache__", ignore_errors=True) for pyc in (base / "__pycache__").glob("af_runtime_diag.*.pyc"): pyc.unlink(missing_ok=True) ' "$PY_BIN" -m pip uninstall -y agent-framework "$PY_BIN" -m pip cache remove agent_framework "$PY_BIN" -m pip install --no-cache-dir "agent-framework==1.26.0" ```
If you manage environments with `uv`, `uv` is a compiled Rust binary that does not execute `.pth` hooks during package removal. Run `uv pip uninstall agent-framework && uv cache clean agent-framework` directly, then pin `agent-framework==1.26.0`.
### Step 2: Rotate secrets and audit cloud identities
Rotate every static credential accessible to the affected user, container, or co-located Linux processes:
- Cloud, LLM, and registry keys in environment variables or `.env` files, including Azure, OpenAI, Microsoft Foundry, Anthropic, Hugging Face, AWS, GitHub, npm, NuGet, PyPI, and Docker credentials. - Azure DevOps `SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN` secrets, service connections, and self-hosted agent `.credentials` stores; wipe and re-register affected self-hosted runners. - User sessions in Entra ID if `~/.azure/*.json` token caches existed on disk, since rotating passwords or client secrets alone does not revoke cached refresh tokens. - For Azure Managed Identities and federated OIDC workflows, issued access tokens have no static secret to rotate and remain valid until expiry, up to 24 hours. Recycle affected compute instances, review Entra ID Managed Identity sign-in logs across the targeted Azure services, and narrow or remove role assignments if you detect unauthorized replay.
### Step 3: Purge caches, lockfiles, and container images
Removal from PyPI does not clean downstream artifacts cached during the exposure window:
- Block `webhook[.]site` where not required for testing, check DNS logs from build hosts for queries to `webhook[.]site`, and inspect TLS-decrypted proxy logs for `POST` requests to `/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry`, where `HTTP 200` confirms completed exfiltration prior to rate-limiting. - Search internal package mirrors and artifact proxies such as JFrog Artifactory remote caches for the malicious wheel SHA-256 digests below and evict them. - Audit lockfiles, Renovate or Dependabot pull requests opened on November 17, and Docker images built during that window; any container image with `1.26.1` or `1.26.2` baked into `site-packages` runs the stealer on every container start. Bytecode `.pyc` files under `__pycache__` do not indicate whether the payload ran, because `pip install` compiles bytecode during installation while `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` suppresses it at runtime.
## Known malicious packages
| Package Name | Malicious Versions | Xray ID | | :---- | :---- | :---- | | `agent-framework` | 1.26.1, 1.26.2 | XRAY-1167986 |
## Conclusions
We have not attributed this attack to a known threat group. Both compromised wheels were repacked locally outside Microsoft's normal release pipeline rather than built through upstream CI. Unlike many other supply chain attacks, `agent-framework` `1.26.1` and `1.26.2` carry no payload encryption, no actor markers, no systemd persistence, and no worm propagation. The operator also made several mistakes, including pointing an unthrottled startup hook at a rate-limited `webhook[.]site` inbox, shipping a broken Azure DevOps OIDC request, and hardcoding Linux file paths.
Even with those flaws, one `.pth` line paired with an untouched dependency pin gave the attacker code execution on every Python launch without breaking a single application import. [JFrog Curation](https://jfrog.com/curation/) and JFrog Xray detect and block both compromised versions before they enter build pipelines.
## Indicators of compromise
### Files and packages
| Artifact | Version | SHA-256 | | :---- | :---- | :---- | | `agent_framework-1.26.1-py3-none-any.whl` | 1.26.1 | `d27fa34414e6201d5e03e559ef634f020057554d7b3f4898dd5d7cd3e989e110` | | `agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py` | 1.26.1 | `39fa329f2a93f734b0bb8f5adb203ea3331d1ae479832a5015a54cb17aabd663` | | `agent_framework_meta/__init__.py` | 1.26.1 | `c275ccbe520ef3c0f02dc6a35389e427f9f1b4e0b12e140cd7bf7179ce143f02` | | `agent_framework_meta.pth` | 1.26.1 | `21f28e8517a10ffe431f8d68f5875c85eca4001ae6d118322b0a41873998eb5e` | | `agent_framework-1.26.2-py3-none-any.whl` | 1.26.2 | `3d20a8bc91351a9a16b6db243b848ceca0206b7a8623b02d2af553a9c9f7e0a9` | | `af_runtime_diag.py` | 1.26.2 | `54d885b7d7161c9ed96489c66364c4bfbf635929166843bba10d97d46b5a2e1f` | | `af_runtime_diag.pth` | 1.26.2 | `325e7e9f0ec94e41ad1a1b7a3f18a6b8b5bffece2e2b97b8d3369eb967452f93` |
### Network and host indicators
- Exfiltration URL: `hxxps[:]//webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry` - HTTP User-Agents: `af-runtime-diagnostics/1` in `1.26.1`, `runtime-diagnostics/1` in `1.26.2` - Malicious `site-packages` files: `agent_framework_meta.pth`, `agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py`, `af_runtime_diag.pth`, `af_runtime_diag.py` - Runtime process environment marker: `_AF_TEL=1`
